title: Deciding the two-quantifier theory of c.e. degrees
formal: Is the set of true universal-existential sentences of the pure order R decidable?
definitions:
A set A of natural numbers is computably enumerable (c.e.) if a finite ordinary Turing program enumerates exactly A. Write A≤_T B when an oracle Turing machine with membership access to B decides membership in A on every input. Equivalence under mutual reducibility defines a Turing degree. R is the set of degrees containing a c.e. set, ordered by ≤_T; it is not the set of all degrees below the halting problem. All quantification over degrees below is over R. The language has only ≤ and logical equality, with no named degrees or parameters unless explicitly stated.

Input is a finite encoded sentence ∀x1…∀xr ∃y1…∃ys θ, where r,s≥0 are arbitrary finite integers and θ is any Boolean combination of atoms u≤v and u=v in these variables. There are no constants, function symbols or hidden quantifiers. Fix any effective finite-string encoding of formulas; malformed strings may be rejected. Decidable means one ordinary Turing program halts on every input and answers whether the sentence is true in the specified structure; there is no complexity bound.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the proposition or its negation, with exactly the structures and quantifiers specified here. A decision procedure must handle arbitrarily long quantifier blocks and matrices; an undecidability proof must concern this fragment itself.
context: The 2022 problem statement separates the unresolved two-quantifier level from decidable one-quantifier and undecidable three-quantifier levels.
why: This locates an important decidability boundary below the known undecidability of the full theory.

import_provenance.original_title: Deciding the two-quantifier theory of c.e. degrees
import_provenance.original_statement: Is the ∀∃ fragment of the first-order theory of computably enumerable Turing degrees decidable in the language containing only the ordering relation? Harrington–Shelah proved the full theory undecidable, but locating the exact boundary between decidable and undecidable fragments remains open.
import_provenance.supplied_caveat: Remark: Editorial continuation of their undecidability theorem. Adding join or meet operations changes the question and can make the two-quantifier fragment undecidable.
